pages.question: A public health physician is reviewing chronic disease data for a county with a predominantly rural, low-income population. The county has among the highest rates of cardiovascular disease mortality and type 2 diabetes in the state. Survey data reveal that residents consume significantly more sodium, saturated fat, and sugar-sweetened beverages than recommended, and far fewer fruits and vegetables. The county has no public transportation, limited grocery store access, and the majority of residents rely on SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) benefits. A community health coalition asks the physician to recommend a public policy intervention targeting dietary behavior at the population level. Which of the following represents the most effective and evidence-supported policy strategy for improving dietary quality and reducing cardiovascular and metabolic disease disparities in this population?

answers.text: Implementing SNAP incentive matching programs to increase purchasing power for fruits and vegetables among low-income residents
Distributing free multivitamin supplements to all SNAP recipients in the county
Implementing a sugar-sweetened beverage excise tax at the county level
Partnering with fast-food chains to offer discounted heart-healthy menu options with reduced sodium and saturated fat
Requiring all county residents to complete an annual dietary assessment and counseling session at the health department

pages.question: A public health physician is reviewing chronic disease data for a county with a predominantly rural, low-income population. The county has among the highest rates of cardiovascular disease mortality and type 2 diabetes in the state. Survey data reveal that residents consume significantly more sodium, saturated fat, and sugar-sweetened beverages than recommended, and far fewer fruits and vegetables. The county has no public transportation, limited grocery store access, and the majority of residents rely on SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) benefits. A community health coalition asks the physician to recommend a public policy intervention targeting dietary behavior at the population level. Which of the following represents the most effective and evidence-supported policy strategy for improving dietary quality and reducing cardiovascular and metabolic disease disparities in this population?

answers.text:
Implementing SNAP incentive matching programs to increase purchasing power for fruits and vegetables among low-income residents
(100%)

Distributing free multivitamin supplements to all SNAP recipients in the county
(0%)

Implementing a sugar-sweetened beverage excise tax at the county level
(0%)

Partnering with fast-food chains to offer discounted heart-healthy menu options with reduced sodium and saturated fat
(0%)

Requiring all county residents to complete an annual dietary assessment and counseling session at the health department
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
SNAP incentive programs such as Double Up Food Bucks, which match SNAP dollars spent on fruits and vegetables at participating retailers, represent one of the strongest evidence-based population-level policies for improving dietary quality among food-insecure adults. These programs simultaneously address both the economic and geographic barriers to healthy food access and have demonstrated significant increases in fruit and vegetable consumption and improved cardiometabolic markers in SNAP-recipient populations. Pairing financial incentives with structural changes — such as expanding SNAP acceptance at farmers' markets and mobile produce vendors — amplifies reach and effectiveness in rural and low-income communities.
(Choice A)
Implementing SNAP incentive matching programs to increase purchasing power for fruits and vegetables among low-income residents
SNAP incentive programs that match benefits spent on fruits and vegetables — such as the Double Up Food Bucks program operating in over 25 states — have robust evidence supporting their effectiveness as population-level dietary interventions. A landmark randomized controlled trial (the Healthy Incentives Pilot) demonstrated that SNAP participants receiving a 30-cent incentive per dollar spent on targeted healthy foods significantly increased fruit and vegetable intake compared with controls. These programs address both the economic barrier (cost of healthy food relative to calorie-dense processed foods) and the geographic barrier when incentives are accepted at farmers' markets and mobile produce vendors in rural areas. For a population that is predominantly SNAP-reliant, this policy has extraordinarily broad reach and directly increases the affordability and availability of the dietary components most associated with cardiovascular and metabolic risk reduction. Furthermore, these programs support local agricultural economies and have demonstrated sustainability through public-private partnerships, making them politically viable and scalable at the county and state levels.
(Choice B)
Distributing free multivitamin supplements to all SNAP recipients in the county
Micronutrient supplementation does not address the core dietary patterns driving cardiovascular and metabolic disease in this population—specifically excess consumption of sodium, saturated fat, and sugar-sweetened beverages combined with inadequate fruit and vegetable intake. While vitamin deficiencies may exist, supplementation does not improve overall dietary quality, reduce consumption of disease-promoting nutrients, or address the fundamental barriers of food access and affordability. This approach treats a secondary issue rather than the primary drivers of chronic disease disparities.
(Choice C)
Implementing a sugar-sweetened beverage excise tax at the county level
Sugar-sweetened beverage taxes have demonstrated efficacy in reducing SSB consumption in urban jurisdictions (e.g., Philadelphia, Berkeley) and can generate revenue for public health programs. However, this intervention faces significant implementation challenges in rural counties where residents may travel to neighboring jurisdictions to purchase beverages, substantially reducing effectiveness. Additionally, SSB taxes are regressive policies that disproportionately burden low-income populations, and this approach addresses only one dietary component rather than comprehensively improving access to healthy whole foods that SNAP-dependent populations need most.
(Choice D)
Partnering with fast-food chains to offer discounted heart-healthy menu options with reduced sodium and saturated fat
While increasing healthy options at fast-food restaurants can be a component of a broader food environment strategy, this approach relies on voluntary corporate participation and consumer choice behavior in a population with limited financial resources. Evidence shows that low-income consumers infrequently select healthier fast-food options due to cost and taste preferences, and this intervention does not address the structural determinants of dietary disparities or the core dietary excesses (sodium, saturated fat, SSBs) driving chronic disease in this community.
(Choice E)
Requiring all county residents to complete an annual dietary assessment and counseling session at the health department
Mandatory dietary assessments are not a recognized public health intervention strategy and have no evidence base for improving dietary behavior or chronic disease outcomes. This approach is administratively burdensome, would face significant compliance barriers in a low-income rural population with limited internet access, and does not address any of the structural or economic determinants of poor dietary quality.

pages.question:
A 24-year-old sexually active woman presents to the clinic with a 4-day history of painful urination and increased urinary frequency. She reports no vaginal discharge, fever, or flank pain. She has had a new sexual partner in the past month and uses condoms inconsistently. Physical examination is unremarkable, including no abdominal tenderness. Lab values are shown below. What is the most appropriate next step in management?



White Blood Cells (Microscopy)	15-20 per HPF
Leukocyte Esterase	Negative
Nitrites	Negative
Bacteria	Absent
Red Blood Cells (Microscopy)	0-2 per HPF
Epithelial Cells	1-2 per HPF
Casts	Absent
Crystals	Absent
Specific Gravity	1.015
pH	6.0
Glucose	Negative
Protein	Negative
Ketones	Negative
Bilirubin	Negative
Urobilinogen	Normal
Urine Culture	No Growth

answers.text:
Administer empirical antibiotics for urinary tract infection
(2.56%)

Prescribe anticholinergic medication for overactive bladder
(0%)

Repeat urine culture with sensitivity testing
(0%)

Perform chlamydia and gonorrhea nucleic acid amplification testing
(94.87%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This sexually active young woman presents with dysuria, urinary frequency, and sterile pyuria (leukocytes in urine without bacteria or positive culture), which is suggestive of Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis. Given the risk of co-infection, nucleic acid amplification testing for both chlamydia and gonorrhea is the best next step.
(Choice A)
Order pelvic ultrasonography
Pelvic ultrasonography is not indicated in this case. The patient presents with isolated urinary symptoms (dysuria and frequency) without any gynecologic complaints such as pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, or missed periods that would suggest ovarian pathology, ectopic pregnancy, or other pelvic abnormalities requiring imaging evaluation.
(Choice B)
Administer empirical antibiotics for urinary tract infection
Empirical antibiotics for UTI would be inappropriate here. Despite the patient's dysuria and frequency symptoms, the negative urine culture, absent bacteria on microscopy, and negative nitrites indicate this is not a typical bacterial UTI. The presence of sterile pyuria (elevated WBCs without bacteria) in a sexually active woman suggests urethritis from a non-culturable pathogen like chlamydia.
(Choice C)
Prescribe anticholinergic medication for overactive bladder
Anticholinergic medication for overactive bladder is inappropriate here. While anticholinergics can reduce urinary frequency, they do not address infectious causes of urethritis. The patient's sterile pyuria and recent sexual activity strongly suggest an infectious etiology that requires antimicrobial treatment, not symptomatic management of bladder dysfunction.
(Choice D)
Repeat urine culture with sensitivity testing
Repeating the urine culture is unnecessary, as the initial culture was negative, and the pyuria is likely due to a non-culturable pathogen like chlamydia.
(Choice E)
Perform chlamydia and gonorrhea nucleic acid amplification testing
This is the correct next step, as dysuria with sterile pyuria in a sexually active woman is classic for chlamydial urethritis, and testing for gonorrhea is also indicated due to common co-infection.

pages.question:
A 38-year-old woman visits the clinic with frequent morning headaches, episodes of dizziness, and occasional confusion. She works in a bakery located downstairs with minimal ventilation. She doesn't smoke or drink alcohol, but mentions feeling unusually tired lately. Physical examination reveals normal heart sounds and a benign abdominal exam. 

Initial laboratory findings: 
Hematocrit 61%
White Blood Cell count 6,800/mm³
Platelets 210,000/mm³. 

What is the most plausible cause of her increased hematocrit?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's work environment in a poorly ventilated bakery suggests potential carbon monoxide exposure, which could explain her neurological symptoms (headaches, dizziness, confusion, fatigue). However, CO exposure does not cause polycythemia. The elevated hematocrit requires further investigation for other causes of secondary polycythemia (such as sleep apnea, chronic lung disease) or primary polycythemia vera.
(Choice A)
Dehydration
Dehydration causes hemoconcentration, which can elevate hematocrit by reducing plasma volume rather than increasing RBC mass. However, the patient lacks typical signs of dehydration such as altered mental status, poor skin turgor, or orthostatic hypotension.
(Choice B)
High altitude exposure
Chronic exposure to high altitude (>2500m) stimulates erythropoietin production due to reduced atmospheric oxygen, leading to secondary polycythemia. This patient has no history of high altitude residence or recent travel to mountainous regions.
(Choice C)
Renal artery stenosis
Renal artery stenosis can cause increased erythropoietin production via renal hypoxia, but this condition is rare and remains unsupported by the patient's particulars.
(Choice D)
Carbon monoxide exposure
Carbon monoxide exposure causes carboxyhemoglobin formation, which reduces oxygen-carrying capacity but does not cause polycythemia or elevated hematocrit. CO poisoning typically presents with normal hematocrit levels. The symptoms described could be from CO exposure, but this would not explain the elevated hematocrit.
(Choice E)
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
While COPD can induce compensatory polycythemia due to chronic hypoxia, this is highly unlikely as the patient shows no respiratory symptoms typically associated with COPD.

pages.question: A 50-year-old woman with a longstanding history of chronic hepatitis C infection presents with fatigue and joint pain persisting over two weeks. On examination, she has mild hepatomegaly, no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease, and her vitals are stable. Laboratory analysis shows alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 142 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 116 IU/L, and a total bilirubin of 2.1 mg/dL. What additional clinical condition might you anticipate in this patient?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Chronic hepatitis C infection commonly causes extrahepatic manifestations through cryoglobulinemia, an immune complex-mediated process. Mixed cryoglobulinemia leads to immune complex deposition in various organs, most notably the kidneys, causing membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN). This renal complication presents with proteinuria, hematuria, and often hypertension, and should be suspected in hepatitis C patients with systemic symptoms like fatigue and arthralgia.
(Choice A)
Pancreatitis
Pancreatitis is not a recognized extrahepatic manifestation of chronic hepatitis C infection. The elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin indicate hepatic involvement rather than pancreatic pathology.
(Choice B)
Hemolytic anemia
Hemolytic anemia is not a typical extrahepatic manifestation of hepatitis C. While hepatitis C can cause cytopenias through hypersplenism or interferon treatment, autoimmune hemolytic anemia is not characteristically associated with this infection.
(Choice C)
Polymyositis
While polymyositis can rarely be associated with hepatitis C through autoimmune mechanisms, it is not a well-established or common extrahepatic manifestation. The patient's joint pain is more likely related to cryoglobulinemia-associated arthralgia.
(Choice D)
Peripheral neuropathy
While peripheral neuropathy can occur in hepatitis C patients, particularly in the setting of cryoglobulinemia, it is less common than renal involvement (MPGN). The patient's presentation with fatigue and joint pain more strongly suggests cryoglobulinemia with renal manifestations.
(Choice E)
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
MPGN is linked to chronic hepatitis C due to cryoglobulinemia, characterized by proteinuria and hematuria. It is a common renal manifestation associated with the infection.

pages.question: A 35-year-old elementary school teacher presents to the emergency department with a 2-week history of worsening shortness of breath, especially when lying flat, and swelling in his legs. He reports a recent episode of fever, cough, and fatigue about a month ago, which he attributed to a 'bad cold' circulating among his students. He has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. Physical examination reveals jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, an S3 gallop, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Echocardiogram shows a dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction of 30% and global hypokinesis. Electrocardiogram demonstrates nonspecific ST-T wave changes. A chest X-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's cardiomyopathy?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has dilated cardiomyopathy most likely due to viral myocarditis, a common etiology in young adults following a recent viral illness, presenting with decompensated heart failure symptoms, echocardiographic findings of ventricular dilation and reduced ejection fraction, and nonspecific ECG changes. Other causes such as coronary artery disease, fungal infection, autoimmune disease, thyroid dysfunction, tick-borne illness, and alcohol abuse are less likely given the acute onset after a viral prodrome and absence of risk factors.
(Choice A)
Ischemic cardiomyopathy
Ischemic cardiomyopathy is unlikely in this 35-year-old patient without cardiovascular risk factors. Additionally, the global hypokinesis pattern on echocardiogram (rather than regional wall motion abnormalities) suggests a non-ischemic etiology.
(Choice B)
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroid cardiomyopathy typically presents with bradycardia, diastolic dysfunction, and systemic hypothyroid symptoms (weight gain, fatigue, cold intolerance). The acute onset following viral illness and absence of these features makes hypothyroidism unlikely.
(Choice C)
Autoimmune myocarditis
Systemic lupus erythematosus can cause myocarditis, but this patient lacks other features like rash, joint pain, or serologic evidence of autoimmune disease.
(Choice D)
Viral infection
Viral myocarditis is a common cause of dilated cardiomyopathy in young adults, often following a recent viral illness, leading to heart failure symptoms and echocardiographic findings as described.
(Choice E)
Coccidioidomycosis
Coccidioidomycosis can cause myocarditis but is geographically limited to endemic areas (southwestern US) and typically requires specific exposure history. The temporal relationship with a recent viral illness makes this fungal etiology less likely.

pages.question: A 35-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after a nonfatal drowning incident while kayaking in a river. She was submerged briefly, aspirated water, and was rescued by companions. She coughed up some water on site and now reports feeling fine. On examination, she is alert and asymptomatic, with normal vital signs, clear lung sounds, and normal oxygen saturation. A chest x-ray is shown below. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text:
Admit to the hospital for observation
(75.47%)

Discharge home with instructions to return if symptoms worsen
(24.53%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient experienced nonfatal drowning and is currently asymptomatic with normal vital signs and examination. However, she remains at risk for delayed pulmonary complications such as pulmonary edema, ARDS, or secondary drowning syndrome within the first 8-24 hours post-incident. Current guidelines recommend admission for close observation for at least 8 hours, with serial clinical assessments and repeat chest imaging if symptoms develop. Patients can be discharged if they remain asymptomatic with normal vital signs and chest X-ray after the observation period.
(Choice A)
Administer prophylactic antibiotics and discharge
This is incorrect because prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely indicated after freshwater drowning unless there are signs of infection or contaminated water exposure. More importantly, the patient still requires observation regardless of antibiotic administration due to the risk of delayed pulmonary complications.
(Choice B)
Admit to the hospital for observation
This is correct. Even asymptomatic patients after nonfatal drowning need monitoring for at least 8 hours due to the risk of delayed pulmonary edema or other complications.
(Choice C)
Obtain immediate pulmonary function tests
This is incorrect because pulmonary function tests are not part of the acute management of drowning victims. The priority is clinical observation for delayed complications such as pulmonary edema or ARDS, which are better monitored through serial clinical assessments and repeat chest imaging if needed.
(Choice D)
Discharge home with instructions to return if symptoms worsen
This is incorrect because even asymptomatic patients after nonfatal drowning require observation for at least 8 hours due to the risk of delayed pulmonary complications such as pulmonary edema, ARDS, or secondary drowning syndrome, which can develop hours after the initial incident.

pages.question: A 40-year-old woman with a known history of systemic lupus erythematosus presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and chest pain. Imaging is shown below. She has a history of three unexplained miscarriages in the second trimester. Laboratory tests show a positive lupus anticoagulant. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her pulmonary embolism?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This woman with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with a pulmonary embolism and a history of recurrent miscarriages, along with a positive lupus anticoagulant. These findings are characteristic of antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), which causes thrombotic events and pregnancy morbidity in the presence of specific autoantibodies. Other causes of hypercoagulability are less likely given the association with SLE and the specific antibody positivity. The CT scan shows a large pulmonary embolism at the bifurcation of the pulmonary artery (saddle embolism).
(Choice A)
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
This is incorrect. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) can cause thrombotic complications due to complement-mediated platelet activation and hemolysis. However, PNH typically presents with hemolytic anemia, hemoglobinuria (especially nocturnal), and pancytopenia. This patient lacks these hematologic manifestations and has findings specific to antiphospholipid syndrome (SLE, lupus anticoagulant, pregnancy morbidity).
(Choice B)
Antiphospholipid syndrome
This is correct. The patient's history of SLE, recurrent miscarriages, pulmonary embolism, and positive lupus anticoagulant fulfill the criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome, which is a common cause of thrombosis in SLE patients.
(Choice C)
Factor V Leiden mutation
This is incorrect. While Factor V Leiden mutation is a common inherited thrombophilia that can cause pulmonary embolism, it does not explain this patient's constellation of findings. Factor V Leiden is not specifically associated with SLE, lupus anticoagulant positivity, or the pattern of recurrent second-trimester pregnancy losses seen in antiphospholipid syndrome.
(Choice D)
Disseminated intravascular coagulation
This is incorrect. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a consumptive coagulopathy characterized by simultaneous thrombosis and bleeding due to consumption of clotting factors and platelets. DIC typically presents acutely with bleeding manifestations, low platelets, prolonged coagulation studies, and elevated fibrin degradation products. This patient has isolated thrombosis with a chronic autoimmune condition, which is characteristic of antiphospholipid syndrome, not DIC.
(Choice E)
Protein C deficiency
This is incorrect. Protein C deficiency is an inherited thrombophilia that can cause venous thromboembolism, but it does not explain this patient's specific clinical presentation. Unlike antiphospholipid syndrome, protein C deficiency is not associated with SLE, positive lupus anticoagulant, or the characteristic pattern of recurrent second-trimester pregnancy losses.

pages.question: During an evening clinic, a 3-day-old female infant is brought in by her father because of constant vomiting and lethargy. The baby has not passed stool since birth, and her abdomen appears markedly distended. During the physical examination, there is an absence of stool on digital rectal exam. Hirschsprung disease is on your differential diagnosis, and you plan for abdominal ultrasonography and a contrast enema. However, the father expresses significant hesitation and denies further diagnostic interventions, insisting the child appears normal. How should you proceed?

answers.text:
Obtain immediate ethics consultation and legal guidance
(4.49%)

Gently explain the medical necessity and proceed with the tests
(87.18%)

Contact social services about parental refusal
(1.92%)

Schedule a multidisciplinary team meeting to discuss the case
(2.56%)

Respect the father's wishes and omit testing
(3.85%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Suspected Hirschsprung disease in a neonate requires prompt evaluation, but the approach to parental refusal of diagnostic testing involves careful consideration of the immediacy of risk, thorough informed consent discussion, and potentially ethics consultation. While failure to pass meconium is concerning and can lead to complications, the situation typically allows time for proper consent processes rather than immediate override of parental wishes. True medical emergencies requiring immediate intervention without consent are reserved for situations with imminent life-threatening complications.
(Choice A)
Obtain immediate ethics consultation and legal guidance
While ethics and legal consultation may be appropriate in complex cases of parental refusal, in truly emergent situations requiring immediate intervention, treatment should not be delayed for consultations. However, this scenario may not represent such an emergency.
(Choice B)
Gently explain the medical necessity and proceed with the tests
While Hirschsprung disease can lead to serious complications if untreated, it is not typically an immediate emergency requiring override of parental consent. The appropriate approach involves thorough discussion of risks and benefits, involvement of ethics committee if needed, and following institutional protocols for situations where parents refuse recommended care. Emergency override of parental consent is reserved for truly life-threatening situations requiring immediate intervention.
(Choice C)
Contact social services about parental refusal
Involving appropriate support services, including ethics consultation and potentially child protective services, may be warranted when parents refuse medically necessary care. This is often a more appropriate step than immediately overriding parental consent, especially when the situation is not immediately life-threatening.
(Choice D)
Schedule a multidisciplinary team meeting to discuss the case
Extended family involvement in medical decision-making is not appropriate without proper legal authority. Additionally, in cases requiring urgent medical attention, time-consuming family meetings could delay necessary care.
(Choice E)
Respect the father's wishes and omit testing
Simply respecting parental wishes without further action is inappropriate when a serious medical condition is suspected. However, this doesn't mean immediately overriding consent, but rather engaging in proper informed consent discussion, ethics consultation, and following institutional protocols.

pages.question:
A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset of shortness of breath, chest pain, and palpitations after a long-haul flight. He has a respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute. Physical examination reveals perioral numbness and carpopedal spasm. Lab values are shown below. Which of the following best explains the observed decrease in ionized calcium?



WBC Count	7200 /µL
Hemoglobin	13.5 g/dL
Hematocrit	40 %
RBC Count	4.6 million/µL
Platelet Count	250000 /µL
Arterial pH	7.50
PaCO2	25 mm Hg
PaO2	85 mm Hg
Serum Sodium	140 mEq/L
Serum Potassium	4.2 mEq/L
Serum Chloride	103 mEq/L
Serum Bicarbonate (HCO3-)	24 mEq/L
Total Calcium	9.2 mg/dL
Ionized Calcium	3.8 mg/dL
Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)	15 mg/dL
Serum Creatinine	0.9 mg/dL
AST (SGOT)	28 U/L
ALT (SGPT)	32 U/L
Alkaline Phosphatase	90 U/L
Total Bilirubin	0.8 mg/dL
Albumin	4.2 g/dL
Total Protein	7.1 g/dL

answers.text:
Increase in calcium bound to albumin
(73.24%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient presents with respiratory alkalosis secondary to hyperventilation, likely due to pulmonary embolism following a long flight. The elevated pH (7.50) and low PaCO2 (25 mmHg) cause hydrogen ions to dissociate from albumin binding sites, allowing more calcium to bind to albumin. This reduces the ionized (physiologically active) calcium fraction while total calcium remains normal, producing symptoms of functional hypocalcemia including perioral numbness and carpopedal spasm.
(Choice A)
Increase in calcium bound to albumin
Respiratory alkalosis increases pH, causing hydrogen ions to dissociate from albumin, which then binds more calcium, reducing ionized calcium levels.
(Choice B)
Intracellular shift of calcium
Calcium does not significantly shift intracellularly in response to alkalosis; this is more characteristic of potassium in alkalotic states.
(Choice C)
Decreased parathyroid hormone secretion
PTH secretion would actually be stimulated by low ionized calcium levels, but this is a compensatory response, not the cause. The primary mechanism here is the immediate effect of alkalosis on calcium-albumin binding, which occurs within minutes, before hormonal responses can take effect.
(Choice D)
Decrease in total serum calcium
Total calcium is normal at 9.2 mg/dL, which rules out true hypocalcemia. The isolated decrease in ionized calcium with normal total calcium indicates a binding/complexation issue rather than an absolute calcium deficiency.
(Choice E)
Intracellular calcium shift
Acute respiratory alkalosis does not directly cause increased renal calcium excretion; this is seen in conditions like hyperparathyroidism or diuretic use.

pages.question: A 58-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents to his primary care physician complaining of cramping pain in his buttocks and thighs that occurs predictably after walking up inclines or stairs. The pain resolves with a few minutes of rest. He has no history of back pain or neurological symptoms. Vital signs are normal. Examination shows normal muscle strength and sensation in the lower extremities, but pedal pulses are diminished bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has risk factors for atherosclerosis (smoking) and symptoms consistent with intermittent claudication due to aortoiliac peripheral arterial disease. The next step in management is to obtain physiologic testing with ankle-brachial index (ABI) to confirm peripheral arterial disease (PAD). ABI is a noninvasive vascular test and a ratio of systolic blood pressure at the ankle to brachial artery, diagnostic for PAD if ≤ 0.90. Other testing or interventions should be considered only after confirming PAD with ABI.
(Choice A)
Duplex ultrasonography
Duplex ultrasonography can localize lesions but is not the first-line test; it is typically used after ABI confirms PAD.
(Choice B)
Ankle-brachial index
Ankle-brachial index is the preferred initial noninvasive test to diagnose peripheral arterial disease in symptomatic patients, as it is highly sensitive and specific.
(Choice C)
Electromyography
Electromyography assesses neuromuscular function but is not indicated here, as symptoms suggest vascular etiology rather than neuropathy.
(Choice D)
Magnetic resonance angiography
Magnetic resonance angiography is not invasive but is more expensive and time-consuming than ABI. It is typically reserved for pre-procedural planning when revascularization is being considered, after PAD has been confirmed and conservative management has failed.
(Choice E)
Lumbar spine MRI
Lumbar spine MRI would evaluate for neurogenic claudication due to spinal stenosis, but this patient's presentation is more consistent with vascular claudication. Key distinguishing features include the absence of back pain, normal neurological examination, and most importantly, diminished pedal pulses bilaterally, which strongly suggests peripheral arterial disease.

pages.question: A 35-year-old woman with no current medical diagnoses presents for a wellness visit. Her BMI is 23.4 kg/m², blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, and her fasting glucose and lipids are normal. She reports eating a diet she describes as consisting of approximately 70% ultraprocessed foods — primarily convenience meals, packaged snacks, sweetened beverages, and fast food — due to her demanding work schedule and budget constraints. She is motivated to improve her diet but says she has very little time to cook and limited finances. She asks for practical advice on reducing ultraprocessed food intake within her real-world constraints. Which of the following represents the most practically applicable and evidence-based counseling for reducing ultraprocessed food intake in a time- and budget-constrained patient?

answers.text:
Recommend that she subscribe to a meal kit delivery service providing pre-portioned fresh ingredients to eliminate preparation time while avoiding ultraprocessed foods
(0%)

Recommend practical minimally processed substitutions within her time and budget constraints: plain canned beans, lentils, and eggs as inexpensive protein sources; plain frozen vegetables as nutritionally equivalent to fresh with no preparation waste; plain oats as a quick low-cost breakfast alternative to ultraprocessed cereals; and batch cooking whole grains and legumes once weekly to provide quick meals throughout the week
(100%)

Advise her to eliminate all convenience foods immediately and commit to cooking all meals from scratch using fresh whole ingredients, as partial reduction of ultraprocessed food intake produces no meaningful health benefit
(0%)

Advise the patient that reducing ultraprocessed food intake is not feasible within time and budget constraints and that her current dietary pattern is acceptable given her normal metabolic parameters
(0%)

Since her current metabolic parameters are normal, defer dietary counseling until she develops a diet-related chronic disease when motivation for change will be higher
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Practical strategies for reducing ultraprocessed food intake under time and budget constraints include: plain canned beans and lentils as inexpensive minimally processed protein sources; frozen plain vegetables as nutritionally equivalent to fresh at lower cost and with zero waste; plain oats, eggs, and plain yogurt as quick minimally processed alternatives to breakfast cereals and flavored yogurts; and batch cooking whole grains and legumes once weekly. These strategies do not require expensive specialty foods or extensive cooking time, and address the real-world barriers that drive ultraprocessed food reliance.
(Choice A)
Recommend that she subscribe to a meal kit delivery service providing pre-portioned fresh ingredients to eliminate preparation time while avoiding ultraprocessed foods
Meal kit delivery services typically cost $10–15 per meal per person — a significant financial burden for a budget-constrained patient. This recommendation directly conflicts with her explicitly stated financial constraints and is not practically applicable to her circumstances. Effective counseling for budget-constrained patients should identify the least expensive minimally processed foods such as canned legumes, eggs, frozen vegetables, and plain oats, not premium services that are financially inaccessible.
(Choice B)
Recommend practical minimally processed substitutions within her time and budget constraints: plain canned beans, lentils, and eggs as inexpensive protein sources; plain frozen vegetables as nutritionally equivalent to fresh with no preparation waste; plain oats as a quick low-cost breakfast alternative to ultraprocessed cereals; and batch cooking whole grains and legumes once weekly to provide quick meals throughout the week
Effective ultraprocessed food reduction counseling must engage with the real-world structural factors that drive ultraprocessed food reliance — time constraints and budget limitations — rather than prescribing idealized dietary patterns that are impractical for this patient's circumstances. Understanding why ultraprocessed foods dominate time-constrained, budget-limited diets: Ultraprocessed foods are engineered for convenience (long shelf life, no preparation required, portable, calorie-dense), affordability (often cheaper per calorie than fresh whole foods due to industrialized production and government commodity subsidies for refined ingredient crops), and palatability (hyperpalatable flavor engineering promotes repeat purchase). Addressing time constraints with minimally processed alternatives: (1) Plain canned beans (black beans, chickpeas, kidney beans in water with minimal salt) require zero preparation — rinse and eat. Cost approximately $0.80–1.50 per can providing three to four servings of protein and fiber. Versus ultraprocessed alternative: packaged seasoned bean products with additives. (2) Frozen plain vegetables (broccoli, peas, spinach, edamame) are nutritionally equivalent to fresh in most micronutrients, require minimal preparation (microwave in three minutes), produce zero waste from spoilage, and cost less than fresh per serving. (3) Eggs are minimally processed, quick to prepare (scrambled in three minutes), inexpensive ($0.20–0.35 per egg), and provide high-quality protein. Versus ultraprocessed alternative: protein bars ($2–5 each with long ingredient lists). (4) Plain rolled oats require five minutes of preparation, cost pennies per serving, and provide fiber and protein. Versus ultraprocessed alternative: flavored instant oatmeal packets with added sugar and artificial flavor. (5) Plain Greek yogurt (minimally processed) provides protein and probiotics. Versus ultraprocessed alternative: flavored yogurt with added sugars. Batch cooking strategy: Cooking one large pot of brown rice, quinoa, or lentils once weekly (30 minutes) provides the base for multiple quick meals throughout the week — reducing the time barrier to minimally processed eating. Budget considerations: The cheapest minimally processed foods per gram of protein — dried lentils ($0.25–0.40 per serving), dried beans, eggs, canned fish, plain oats — are often less expensive than their ultraprocessed counterparts when cost per serving is compared rather than cost per package.
(Choice C)
Advise her to eliminate all convenience foods immediately and commit to cooking all meals from scratch using fresh whole ingredients, as partial reduction of ultraprocessed food intake produces no meaningful health benefit
Complete immediate elimination of all convenience foods is an impractical all-or-nothing prescription for a patient with genuine time and financial constraints, and is likely to produce brief compliance followed by complete return to baseline — consistent with behavior change evidence showing that extreme prescriptions produce worse long-term outcomes than gradual achievable changes. Furthermore, the evidence does support dose-response relationships between ultraprocessed food reduction and health outcomes — partial reduction does produce meaningful benefit. Counseling should identify achievable first steps within her actual constraints.
(Choice D)
Advise the patient that reducing ultraprocessed food intake is not feasible within time and budget constraints and that her current dietary pattern is acceptable given her normal metabolic parameters
Clinical nihilism about dietary improvement in time- and budget-constrained patients is both factually incorrect and therapeutically harmful. Multiple minimally processed foods — canned beans, eggs, frozen vegetables, plain oats — are less expensive per serving than many ultraprocessed alternatives and require minimal preparation time. Additionally, this patient's current normal metabolic parameters do not protect her from the longitudinal health risks associated with high ultraprocessed food consumption. Effective counseling should identify achievable practical strategies rather than accepting dietary status quo based on perceived constraints.
(Choice E)
Since her current metabolic parameters are normal, defer dietary counseling until she develops a diet-related chronic disease when motivation for change will be higher
This approach misses the most valuable and effective window for dietary intervention — primary prevention before chronic disease develops. Changing dietary patterns is considerably more difficult after chronic disease diagnosis when metabolic damage has already occurred, medications are required, and disease management competes with dietary behavior change for patient attention. Primary prevention dietary counseling in a motivated patient without current disease is high-yield clinical work. Additionally, waiting for disease development to provide dietary counseling is not consistent with evidence-based preventive medicine standards.

pages.question: A 35-year-old woman with a 3-year history of ulcerative colitis (UC), currently in remission on mesalamine and infliximab, presents at 8 weeks gestation with her second pregnancy. She reports mild abdominal cramping but no hematochezia or diarrhea. She is concerned about the impact of her UC on the pregnancy and vice versa. Colonoscopy prior to pregnancy confirmed remission. Which of the following statements best describes the management and risks associated with UC in this patient during pregnancy?

answers.text:
Discontinue infliximab immediately due to teratogenic risk, and monitor for UC flare, which is unlikely during pregnancy
(13.11%)

Recommend termination of pregnancy due to inevitable severe UC exacerbation and high miscarriage risk
(0%)

Switch to corticosteroids only, as they are the safest option; UC remission is usually maintained without intervention during pregnancy
(24.59%)

Advise elective cesarean delivery to avoid UC complications; discontinue all medications to minimize fetal exposure
(0%)

Continue mesalamine and infliximab, as they are safe; closely monitor for UC flare, which can worsen during pregnancy and lead to preterm delivery or small for gestational age
(62.3%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This pregnant patient with UC in remission should continue her maintenance medications (mesalamine and infliximab), as both are considered safe during pregnancy. Pregnancy is a high-risk period for UC exacerbation due to placental inflammatory mediators and hormonal changes, which can lead to maternal complications and fetal risks including preterm delivery, low birth weight, and small for gestational age infants. Maintaining disease remission through continued medical therapy and close monitoring is essential for optimal maternal and fetal outcomes.
(Choice A)
Discontinue infliximab immediately due to teratogenic risk, and monitor for UC flare, which is unlikely during pregnancy
This is incorrect. Infliximab is considered safe to continue during pregnancy for UC management (Category B), with benefits typically outweighing risks. Additionally, pregnancy often increases UC flare risk due to inflammatory and hormonal changes, making discontinuation particularly risky.
(Choice B)
Recommend termination of pregnancy due to inevitable severe UC exacerbation and high miscarriage risk
This is incorrect and represents poor counseling. While UC can worsen during pregnancy, it is highly manageable with appropriate medical therapy. Most patients with UC can have successful pregnancies with proper disease control. Termination is never routinely recommended based solely on UC diagnosis, and the risk of severe exacerbation is reduced with maintained remission.
(Choice C)
Switch to corticosteroids only, as they are the safest option; UC remission is usually maintained without intervention during pregnancy
This is incorrect. Corticosteroids are used for flares but not preferred long-term; most UC medications are safe, and pregnancy increases the risk of UC worsening, requiring active management.
(Choice D)
Advise elective cesarean delivery to avoid UC complications; discontinue all medications to minimize fetal exposure
This is incorrect. Delivery mode is not dictated by UC unless active perianal disease; medications should be continued if needed, as uncontrolled UC poses greater risks to the fetus.
(Choice E)
Continue mesalamine and infliximab, as they are safe; closely monitor for UC flare, which can worsen during pregnancy and lead to preterm delivery or small for gestational age
This is correct. Most UC medications, including mesalamine and infliximab, are safe during pregnancy. Pregnancy is a high-risk period for UC flares due to inflammatory changes, potentially causing fetal complications like preterm birth and growth restriction. Remission should be maintained.

pages.question:
A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with profuse watery diarrhea, vomiting, and muscle cramps that began 2 days after returning from a trip to Southeast Asia, where he consumed undercooked seafood. Vital signs show blood pressure of 88/58 mm Hg, heart rate of 112 beats/min, and respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min. Physical examination reveals dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, and decreased skin turgor. Laboratory studies are shown below. Stool culture confirms Vibrio cholerae infection. Which of the following best describes the expected hormonal profile contributing to this patient's hyponatremia?



Sodium	129 mEq/L
Potassium	3.1 mEq/L
Chloride	96 mEq/L
Bicarbonate	17 mEq/L
Blood urea nitrogen	42 mg/dL
Serum creatinine	1.6 mg/dL
Glucose	94 mg/dL
Calcium	9.0 mg/dL
Urine Color	Yellow	(range: Clear to yellow)
Urine Appearance	Concentrated
Urine Specific Gravity	1.030	(range: 1.005–1.030)
Urine Sodium	8 mEq/L	(normal: >20 mEq/L)
Urine Osmolality	650 mOsm/kg	(range: 50–1200 mOsm/kg)
Urine Protein	Negative	(normal: Negative)
Urine Blood	Negative	(normal: Negative)
Urine Red Blood Cells	0–2/HPF	(normal: 0–2/HPF)
Urine White Blood Cells	0–2/HPF	(normal: 0–5/HPF)
Urine Casts	None seen

answers.text:
High renin, high aldosterone, low antidiuretic hormone
(8.97%)

Low renin, high aldosterone, low antidiuretic hormone
(3.85%)

High renin, low aldosterone, high antidiuretic hormone
(6.41%)

High renin, high aldosterone, high antidiuretic hormone
(64.1%)

Low renin, low aldosterone, high antidiuretic hormone
(16.67%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has hypovolemic hyponatremia due to severe volume depletion from cholera-induced secretory diarrhea. Clinical findings (hypotension, tachycardia, poor skin turgor) and laboratory studies (elevated BUN/creatinine ratio of 26:1, low urine sodium of 8 mEq/L, concentrated urine with specific gravity 1.030) confirm significant hypovolemia. The hyponatremia results from activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (promoting sodium retention) combined with nonosmotic ADH release (promoting water retention that exceeds sodium retention), leading to dilutional hyponatremia despite overall volume depletion.
(Choice A)
High renin, high aldosterone, low antidiuretic hormone
This is incorrect. In hypovolemic hyponatremia, ADH is elevated due to nonosmotic stimuli from volume depletion. Even though serum osmolality may be low (which normally suppresses ADH), the hypovolemic stimulus overrides osmotic regulation, leading to continued ADH secretion and water retention that worsens the hyponatremia.
(Choice B)
Low renin, high aldosterone, low antidiuretic hormone
This is incorrect. This combination is physiologically implausible in hypovolemia. Low renin with high aldosterone suggests primary aldosteronism (inappropriate aldosterone excess), while low ADH would be expected in hypervolemic states. This patient's clinical picture and low urine sodium clearly indicate hypovolemia with activation of all volume-preserving hormonal systems.
(Choice C)
High renin, low aldosterone, high antidiuretic hormone
This is incorrect. When renin is elevated due to hypovolemia, it stimulates angiotensin II production, which in turn stimulates aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex. High renin with low aldosterone could suggest adrenal insufficiency, but this patient's concentrated urine and sodium retention pattern indicate normal aldosterone function.
(Choice D)
High renin, high aldosterone, high antidiuretic hormone
This is correct. Hypovolemia stimulates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, increasing renin and aldosterone levels to promote sodium retention. Nonosmotic release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) occurs due to volume depletion, leading to water retention and dilutional hyponatremia.
(Choice E)
Low renin, low aldosterone, high antidiuretic hormone
This is incorrect. Severe hypovolemia, as evidenced by this patient's elevated BUN/creatinine ratio (42/1.6 = 26:1), low urine sodium (8 mEq/L), and concentrated urine, strongly activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Both renin and aldosterone would be markedly elevated to promote sodium and volume retention.

pages.question: A 40-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for a routine health maintenance visit. She has a history of cervical cancer treated with pelvic radiation therapy at age 25. Other medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity (BMI 32 kg/m²), celiac disease, and daily red meat consumption. She takes aspirin daily for cardiovascular protection. The patient asks about colorectal cancer screening. Which of the following factors in her history most strongly supports initiating screening earlier than recommended for the general population?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Prior abdominopelvic radiation therapy significantly increases colorectal cancer risk and warrants earlier screening (typically 5 years post-radiation or age 35-40), while other risk factors like obesity, diabetes, and red meat consumption increase risk but do not change standard screening timing. Aspirin use is protective and celiac disease does not significantly affect colorectal cancer risk.
(Choice A)
Celiac disease
Celiac disease increases the risk of small bowel adenocarcinoma and lymphoma but does not significantly increase colorectal cancer risk. While some studies suggest a modest association, this is not sufficient to warrant earlier screening per current guidelines.
(Choice B)
Aspirin use
Aspirin use is associated with a reduced risk of colorectal cancer and does not warrant earlier screening.
(Choice C)
History of pelvic radiation therapy
Prior abdominopelvic radiation therapy significantly increases the risk of colorectal cancer, with risk beginning 5-10 years after exposure. Current guidelines recommend initiating screening 5 years after radiation therapy or at age 35-40 (depending on the specific guideline), whichever comes later, rather than waiting until age 45-50 as recommended for average-risk individuals.
(Choice D)
Obesity
While obesity (BMI ≥30) is an established risk factor for colorectal cancer, it is not considered sufficient to warrant earlier screening initiation. Current guidelines classify obesity as increasing risk but not enough to change the standard screening age of 45-50 years for average-risk individuals.
(Choice E)
Red meat consumption
High consumption of red meat increases the risk of colorectal cancer but does not change the timing of screening initiation.

pages.question:
A 42-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department by her family due to progressive confusion, rapid deep breathing, and recurrent vomiting over the past 24 hours. She has been noncompliant with her insulin regimen during a recent episode of urinary tract infection. On examination, she is lethargic with a heart rate of 110 bpm, and a blood pressure of 95/60 mmHg. Initial laboratory results are shown below. She has received an initial bolus of 1 liter of 0.9% saline over the first hour. Repeat labs show serum sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 3.8 mEq/L, and glucose 520 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?



WBC Count	9000 /µL
Neutrophils	65 %
Lymphocytes	25 %
Hemoglobin	13.8 g/dL
Hematocrit	41 %
RBC Count	4.7 million/µL
Platelet Count	250000 /µL
Serum Glucose	620 mg/dL
Arterial pH	7.15
Bicarbonate (HCO3-)	12 mEq/L
Anion Gap	22 mEq/L
Serum Ketones	Positive

answers.text:
Switch to 5% dextrose in 0.9% saline and administer subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin
(13.51%)

Switch to 0.45% saline infusion and start intravenous regular insulin
(27.03%)

Administer intravenous bicarbonate and continue 0.9% saline
(10.81%)

Administer oral potassium supplements and switch to lactated Ringer's solution with regular insulin bolus
(45.95%)

Continue 0.9% saline infusion and administer subcutaneous NPH insulin
(2.7%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) evidenced by hyperglycemia (520-620 mg/dL), anion gap metabolic acidosis (pH 7.15, HCO3- 12 mEq/L, anion gap 22), and positive serum ketones, triggered by UTI-induced insulin noncompliance. After initial volume resuscitation with 0.9% saline, the normal serum sodium (138 mEq/L) indicates appropriate fluid balance, warranting transition to 0.45% saline for ongoing hydration to provide free water. Continuous intravenous regular insulin infusion should be initiated immediately since potassium is adequate (3.8 mEq/L >3.3 mEq/L threshold) to reverse ketosis and normalize glucose. Serial electrolyte monitoring, particularly potassium replacement as levels fall with insulin therapy, and treatment of the precipitating UTI are essential components of management.
(Choice A)
Switch to 5% dextrose in 0.9% saline and administer subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin
This is incorrect. Dextrose-containing fluids (D5 0.9% saline) are added only when serum glucose falls to approximately 200-250 mg/dL to prevent hypoglycemia while continuing insulin to clear ketones. At 520 mg/dL, glucose is still significantly elevated. Additionally, subcutaneous insulin has unpredictable absorption in the dehydrated, acidotic DKA patient and lacks the precise titratability needed for acute management.
(Choice B)
Switch to 0.45% saline infusion and start intravenous regular insulin
This is correct. Following initial 0.9% saline bolus with normal serum sodium, 0.45% saline is appropriate for ongoing hydration. Intravenous regular insulin infusion is essential to resolve hyperglycemia and ketosis in DKA.
(Choice C)
Administer intravenous bicarbonate and continue 0.9% saline
This is incorrect. Bicarbonate administration is not routinely recommended in DKA and is reserved only for severe acidosis (pH <6.9) or cases with hemodynamic instability, as it may paradoxically worsen intracellular acidosis and delay ketone clearance. With a pH of 7.15, insulin therapy and fluid resuscitation are sufficient to correct the acidosis. Additionally, fluids should be switched to 0.45% saline given the normal serum sodium level.
(Choice D)
Administer oral potassium supplements and switch to lactated Ringer's solution with regular insulin bolus
This is incorrect. Lactated Ringer's solution is avoided in DKA because lactate metabolism may be impaired in the setting of severe illness and acidosis. Oral potassium supplementation is inappropriate in the acute setting when the patient has altered mental status and vomiting. Insulin should be administered as a continuous infusion (typically 0.1 units/kg/hr) rather than bolus dosing to allow for precise titration and consistent therapeutic effect.
(Choice E)
Continue 0.9% saline infusion and administer subcutaneous NPH insulin
This is incorrect. After initial resuscitation with normal serum sodium (138 mEq/L), fluids should be switched to 0.45% saline to provide free water and prevent hypernatremia during ongoing hydration. NPH insulin has unpredictable absorption and delayed onset, making it inappropriate for acute DKA management where rapid, titratable control is essential; continuous intravenous regular insulin is the standard of care.

pages.question: A 6-week-old female infant is brought to the pediatric clinic by her parents with concerns of low-grade fever, persistent irritability, and decreased movement of the right arm over the past 48 hours. The parents note that the baby becomes extremely fussy when her right arm is manipulated, such as during clothing changes, and she seems to hold the arm still against her body. On physical examination, the infant has a temperature of 38.2°C, and there is mild erythema and swelling around the right shoulder joint with pain on passive range of motion. Laboratory evaluation shows a white blood cell count of 16,500/mm³ with 65% neutrophils and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 55 mm/hr. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This 6-week-old infant presents with fever, irritability particularly during arm manipulation, decreased arm movement, and holding the arm still. Physical exam reveals mild erythema, swelling, and pain on passive motion of the right shoulder. Laboratory findings indicate leukocytosis with neutrophilic predominance and elevated ESR, consistent with an infectious process in the shoulder joint.
(Choice A)
Nonaccidental trauma
Nonaccidental trauma could cause decreased arm movement and pain, but would not explain the systemic signs of infection including fever, leukocytosis with neutrophilia, and elevated ESR. Additionally, the localized erythema and joint swelling with pain on passive motion are characteristic of septic arthritis rather than trauma-related injury.
(Choice B)
Transient synovitis
Transient synovitis (toxic synovitis) typically occurs in children aged 3-8 years, often following a viral upper respiratory infection. It presents with hip pain and limping but is characteristically afebrile with normal or only mildly elevated inflammatory markers. The acute onset with fever, significant leukocytosis, and elevated ESR in a 6-week-old infant strongly suggests septic arthritis rather than transient synovitis.
(Choice C)
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) typically presents with chronic joint symptoms (>6 weeks duration) in older children, often with morning stiffness and gradual onset. The acute presentation with high fever, acute monoarticular involvement, and marked neutrophilic leukocytosis with elevated ESR are characteristic of septic arthritis rather than the chronic inflammatory pattern seen in JIA.
(Choice D)
Septic arthritis
The infant's symptoms of fever, irritability with joint manipulation, pseudoparalysis of the limb, and signs of inflammation on exam, along with supportive lab findings, are classic for septic arthritis in this age group. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent joint damage.
(Choice E)
Osteomyelitis
Osteomyelitis primarily affects bone and typically presents with deep bone pain and metaphyseal tenderness. While it can cause fever and leukocytosis, the prominent joint swelling, erythema, and severe pain specifically with passive range of motion are more characteristic of intra-articular infection (septic arthritis) rather than bone infection.

pages.question: A 62-year-old woman with a history of meningioma is undergoing elective craniotomy in the sitting position for tumor resection. The procedure is performed under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Approximately 30 minutes into the surgery, after the bone flap is removed and the dura is incised, the patient suddenly develops profound hypotension (blood pressure 60/30 mm Hg), tachycardia (heart rate 140 beats/min), hypoxemia (oxygen saturation 85% on 100% FiO2), and a sharp decrease in end-tidal carbon dioxide from 35 mm Hg to 12 mm Hg. A mill-wheel murmur is auscultated over the precordium. Despite immediate resuscitation efforts including Trendelenburg positioning, fluid bolus, and aspiration via central line, the patient progresses to cardiac arrest. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's acute decompensation?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's acute decompensation during neurosurgery in the sitting position is classic for venous air embolism (VAE). The key features include: (1) surgical positioning above heart level allowing air entry into open veins, (2) timing during dural opening when large venous sinuses are exposed, (3) pathognomonic mill-wheel murmur caused by air bubbles churning in the right ventricle, and (4) sharp drop in end-tidal CO2 due to increased dead space from air obstruction in pulmonary circulation. VAE causes right heart strain, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and obstructive shock that can rapidly progress to cardiac arrest.
(Choice A)
Air embolism
Air embolism is the correct diagnosis, as the clinical features including the sitting position, timing during dural opening, sudden hemodynamic collapse, decreased end-tidal CO2, and mill-wheel murmur are classic for venous air embolism causing right heart strain and obstructive shock.
(Choice B)
Pulmonary thromboembolism
Pulmonary thromboembolism can cause similar hemodynamic instability and decreased end-tidal CO2, but the acute timing during dural opening in the sitting position, combined with the pathognomonic mill-wheel murmur (caused by air bubbles in the right ventricle), makes air embolism the more likely diagnosis in this specific surgical context.
(Choice C)
Myocardial infarction
Myocardial infarction can cause hypotension and tachycardia, but would not produce the pathognomonic mill-wheel murmur (caused by air bubbles churning in the right ventricle) or the characteristic sharp drop in end-tidal CO2 seen with air embolism. The timing with dural opening in the sitting position strongly favors air embolism.
(Choice D)
Anaphylactic reaction
Anaphylaxis typically presents with bronchospasm, hypotension, and cutaneous manifestations (urticaria, angioedema). While it can cause cardiovascular collapse, it would not produce the pathognomonic mill-wheel murmur or the isolated sharp drop in end-tidal CO2 seen with air obstruction in the pulmonary circulation.
(Choice E)
Tension pneumothorax
Tension pneumothorax presents with hypotension, hypoxemia, tracheal deviation, unilateral absent breath sounds, and increased peak airway pressures. The mill-wheel murmur is pathognomonic for air embolism (air bubbles in the right ventricle) and would not occur with pneumothorax.

pages.question: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents to her gynecologist with a new vulvar lesion. She has a history of vulvar lichen sclerosus diagnosed 5 years ago, which has been managed with intermittent topical clobetasol. She reports no recent changes in her treatment regimen but notes a solitary, firm, whitish plaque on the right labium majus that has appeared over the past 2 months. The lesion measures approximately 1.5 cm in diameter, is nontender, and does not itch. She denies any vaginal bleeding, discharge, or systemic symptoms. Physical examination confirms a well-circumscribed, indurated white plaque without ulceration or surrounding erythema. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's history of vulvar lichen sclerosus increases her risk for vulvar squamous cell carcinoma. The new unifocal, firm white plaque is concerning for malignancy, and vulvar biopsy is necessary to differentiate between benign lichen sclerosus changes and neoplastic disease, guiding further treatment.
(Choice A)
Systemic antifungal therapy
The clinical presentation lacks features of vulvar candidiasis or other fungal infections (no pruritus, discharge, or satellite lesions). More importantly, antifungal therapy would not address the primary concern of malignant transformation in this high-risk patient with lichen sclerosus.
(Choice B)
Colposcopy of the vulva
Colposcopy with acetic acid may enhance visualization of vulvar lesions and help identify areas for biopsy, but it cannot provide the histologic diagnosis necessary to distinguish between benign lichen sclerosus changes and vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia or invasive carcinoma.
(Choice C)
Vulvar biopsy
Vulvar biopsy is essential to evaluate for vulvar squamous cell carcinoma in a patient with lichen sclerosus and a new suspicious lesion, as it distinguishes between benign and malignant changes.
(Choice D)
Topical clobetasol application
While topical clobetasol is the standard treatment for lichen sclerosus maintenance, a new firm plaque in a patient with established lichen sclerosus raises concern for malignant transformation. Biopsy is required first to rule out vulvar squamous cell carcinoma before attributing the lesion to a flare of the underlying benign condition.
(Choice E)
Observation and follow-up in 3 months
Observation is inappropriate for a new, concerning lesion in a high-risk patient, as delayed diagnosis of vulvar cancer can lead to progression and poorer outcomes.

pages.question:
A 38-year-old woman presents to the gynecology clinic with complaints of intense, cramp-like pelvic pain that began suddenly 24 hours ago, accompanied by moderate vaginal spotting. She reports a long-standing history of heavy and prolonged menstrual periods, often lasting 8-10 days, which have worsened over the past year. She denies any recent sexual activity, trauma, or use of intrauterine devices. On physical examination, her vital signs are stable, but she appears uncomfortable. Speculum examination reveals a smooth, firm, pedunculated mass approximately 3 cm in diameter emerging from the cervical os, with no active bleeding from the mass itself. The cervix appears dilated to about 4 cm. Bimanual examination confirms a mildly enlarged uterus without adnexal tenderness. Laboratory tests are shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? 



Hemoglobin	11.2 g/dL
Hematocrit	34 %
White Blood Cell Count	7.200 /mm³
Platelet Count	265.000 /mm³
Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)	87 fL
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH)	29 pg
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration (MCHC)	33 g/dL
Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW)	13 %
Urine Pregnancy Test	Negative
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has a prolapsed submucosal leiomyoma uteri causing acute labor-like pelvic pain due to cervical dilation as the fibroid protrudes through the cervix. Her history of heavy, prolonged menses is consistent with submucosal fibroids, which can distort the endometrial cavity and lead to menorrhagia. The firm, round mass visible on speculum exam distinguishes it from other causes of pelvic pain and vaginal masses.
(Choice A)
Uterine inversion
Uterine inversion is an obstetric emergency that typically occurs immediately postpartum when the uterine fundus turns inside out. It presents with severe hemorrhage, shock, and the entire uterine fundus may be visible. This patient's presentation of a localized 3-cm firm mass with chronic menorrhagia in a non-pregnant woman is inconsistent with uterine inversion.
(Choice B)
Endometrial polyp
Endometrial polyps are typically smaller, softer, and more friable than fibroids. While they can cause irregular bleeding, they rarely prolapse through a dilated cervix to cause acute cramping pain. The firm, 3-cm mass and history of progressively worsening menorrhagia over a year are more consistent with a submucosal fibroid.
(Choice C)
Cervical carcinoma
Cervical carcinoma typically presents as an irregular, ulcerated, friable mass that bleeds easily on contact. The bleeding pattern is usually postcoital or intermenstrual rather than the heavy, prolonged menses described. Additionally, the smooth, firm characteristics of this 3-cm mass are more consistent with a benign fibroid rather than the irregular, necrotic appearance of cervical cancer.
(Choice D)
Prolapsed submucosal leiomyoma
Submucosal leiomyomas can prolapse through the cervix, causing cervical dilation and labor-like pain, along with heavy menstrual bleeding, matching this patient's presentation.
(Choice E)
Cervical polyp
Cervical polyps arise from the cervical epithelium and are typically small, soft, and friable. They cause postcoital or intermenstrual spotting but do not cause the heavy, prolonged menstrual periods described. Additionally, cervical polyps do not prolapse through the cervix since they originate from it, and they would not cause cervical dilation or acute cramping pain.

pages.question: A 44-year-old woman collapses while hiking in the mountains and is brought to the hospital. An initial exam shows significant bruising around her lower back and abdomen, though she is alert. Imaging reveals no apparent fractures or immediate signs of internal injury. She is discharged with pain relief medications. A week later, she returns with persistent fever, a loss of appetite, and intense abdominal discomfort. What condition might explain her symptoms?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Pancreatic injury from blunt abdominal trauma can have delayed presentation due to its retroperitoneal location. Initial imaging may be normal, but subsequent pancreatic inflammation, pseudocyst formation, or secondary infection can cause fever, abdominal pain, and systemic symptoms days to weeks later.
(Choice A)
Gastric ulcer perforation
Gastric ulcer perforation presents acutely with severe peritoneal signs and free air on imaging. While trauma can cause gastric injury, delayed perforation a week later without initial signs would be extremely unusual.
(Choice B)
Pancreatic injury
The pancreas can sustain damage from blunt trauma, especially if compressed against the spine. Initial scans can miss this injury, which may cause secondary infection, abscess formation, and symptoms like fever and abdominal pain if untreated.
(Choice C)
Small bowel obstruction
Small bowel obstruction typically presents with crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, and distention, with characteristic imaging findings. The fever and systemic symptoms suggest an inflammatory/infectious process rather than mechanical obstruction.
(Choice D)
Liver laceration
Liver laceration typically presents with hemodynamic instability and hemoperitoneum detectable on initial imaging. While delayed bleeding can occur, the combination of fever and systemic symptoms a week later suggests infection/inflammation rather than bleeding complications.
(Choice E)
Ruptured appendix
Appendicitis typically presents with right lower quadrant pain progressing from periumbilical pain. Traumatic appendiceal rupture is rare, and the location of trauma (lower back/upper abdomen) makes appendiceal injury unlikely.

pages.question: A 38-year-old woman who has never smoked presents with a 6-month history of progressive shortness of breath on exertion and a dry cough. She reports no history of asthma, allergies, or occupational exposures. Her family history is notable for her father dying of 'lung disease' at age 50. Physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds at the lung bases. Spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55 and FEV1 of 60% predicted, consistent with obstructive lung disease. Chest CT demonstrates panacinar emphysema predominantly affecting the lower lobes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient likely has alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency, suggested by early-onset emphysema in a non-smoker with characteristic basilar-predominant panacinar emphysema on CT. The family history of early lung disease further supports this diagnosis. Serum AAT level measurement is the appropriate first-line diagnostic test. Other options are inappropriate: sweat chloride testing is for cystic fibrosis (which typically causes upper lobe disease), methacholine challenge is for asthma (reversible obstruction), echocardiogram evaluates cardiac causes, lung biopsy is invasive and unnecessary when non-invasive testing is available, and polysomnography diagnoses sleep disorders unrelated to structural lung changes.
(Choice A)
Lung biopsy
Lung biopsy is an invasive procedure typically reserved for diagnosing unclear interstitial lung diseases or when less invasive testing is inconclusive. In this case, the clinical presentation and imaging findings strongly suggest alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, which can be definitively diagnosed with a simple blood test.
(Choice B)
Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level
Serum AAT level is the appropriate diagnostic test for suspected AAT deficiency in a young non-smoker with basilar-predominant emphysema.
(Choice C)
Transthoracic echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates for cardiac causes of dyspnea like heart failure, but the obstructive spirometry and emphysema on CT point to a primary pulmonary etiology.
(Choice D)
Polysomnography
Polysomnography is used to diagnose sleep disorders like obstructive sleep apnea. While sleep apnea can cause daytime fatigue and dyspnea, it does not cause the structural emphysematous lung changes demonstrated on this patient's CT scan.
(Choice E)
Sweat chloride test
Sweat chloride testing is used to diagnose cystic fibrosis, which typically causes upper lobe-predominant bronchiectasis and obstructive lung disease. However, this patient's lower lobe panacinar emphysema pattern, lack of recurrent infections, and absence of other CF features make cystic fibrosis unlikely.

pages.question: A 58-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with exertional chest discomfort that occurs predictably during brisk walking and resolves with rest. Cardiac catheterization reveals significant coronary artery stenosis, and she is diagnosed with stable angina. Her physician initiates treatment with metoprolol to prevent recurrent symptoms and improve her exercise capacity. The primary mechanism by which this medication achieves its therapeutic effect in this patient is:
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The question involves a woman with stable angina who is prescribed a daily beta blocker (metoprolol) to prevent anginal episodes, focusing on the mechanism of action. The correct answer is decreased myocardial contractility, which contributes to reducing myocardial oxygen demand. Sublingual nitroglycerin may be used as needed for acute relief, but the daily medication prevents episodes by lowering oxygen demand through effects on heart rate and contractility.
(Choice A)
Inhibition of platelet aggregation
This is incorrect. Beta blockers do not affect platelet function or aggregation. Antiplatelet effects are achieved by medications like aspirin (irreversible COX-1 inhibition), clopidogrel (P2Y12 receptor antagonist), or other dedicated antiplatelet agents. Beta blockers work purely on cardiac beta-adrenergic receptors.
(Choice B)
Reduced peripheral vascular resistance
This is incorrect. While beta blockers can reduce blood pressure and peripheral vascular resistance (particularly non-selective beta blockers), this is not their primary anti-anginal mechanism. The anti-anginal benefit comes specifically from reducing myocardial oxygen demand through decreased heart rate and contractility, not from systemic hemodynamic effects.
(Choice C)
Decreased myocardial contractility
This is correct. Beta blockers like metoprolol reduce myocardial oxygen demand primarily through two mechanisms: decreased heart rate (negative chronotropic effect) and decreased myocardial contractility (negative inotropic effect). This reduction in oxygen demand prevents the supply-demand mismatch that causes anginal symptoms during exertion.
(Choice D)
Increased coronary artery vasodilation
This is incorrect. Beta blockers do not cause coronary artery vasodilation. While some beta blockers with vasodilatory properties (like carvedilol) may have mild vasodilatory effects, metoprolol's primary anti-anginal mechanism is reduction of myocardial oxygen demand. Coronary vasodilation is the primary mechanism of nitrates and certain calcium channel blockers.
(Choice E)
Prolonged diastolic filling time
This is incorrect as the primary mechanism. While beta blockers do prolong diastolic filling time by reducing heart rate, this is a secondary benefit. The primary anti-anginal mechanism is the direct reduction in myocardial oxygen demand through decreased contractility and heart rate, not the improved diastolic perfusion from longer diastolic periods.

pages.question: A concerned father visits a family physician with his 10-year-old daughter. He describes her as characteristically rebellious towards family rules and always disruptive in classroom settings. She often loses her temper and engages in heated arguments with peers. On several occasions, she has refused to adhere to requests from teachers and has vandalized school property during an outburst. What is the most fitting diagnosis for the behavior she presents?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
ODD is characterized by a persistent pattern of defiant, argumentative, and hostile behavior toward authority figures, but unlike conduct disorder, it does not involve serious violations of others' rights or major societal norms. Key features include defiance of rules, argumentative behavior with adults, and deliberate annoyance of others.
(Choice A)
Bipolar disorder
Bipolar disorder in children involves distinct episodes of mania or hypomania alternating with depression. While irritability can occur during mood episodes, the persistent pattern of defiant behavior toward authority figures without clear mood episodes is more consistent with ODD than bipolar disorder.
(Choice B)
Intermittent explosive disorder
Intermittent explosive disorder involves recurrent episodes of impulsive, aggressive outbursts that are grossly out of proportion to precipitating stressors, with significant distress or impairment. The behavior described shows a consistent pattern of defiance rather than episodic explosive outbursts.
(Choice C)
Conduct disorder
Conduct disorder involves a consistent pattern of behavior where societal rules and the rights of others are violated, including aggression toward people/animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness/theft, and serious rule violations. While this child shows defiance and some property damage, the behavior pattern described is more consistent with authority conflicts rather than the severe rights violations characteristic of conduct disorder.
(Choice D)
Oppositional defiant disorder
Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) is typified by a persistent pattern of defiant, argumentative, and hostile behaviors toward authority figures without severely infringing upon the rights of others.
(Choice E)
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
ADHD manifests as inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity but does not primarily involve the pattern of defiant, argumentative behavior toward authority figures described in this case. While ADHD can co-occur with ODD, the core symptoms here reflect oppositional behaviors rather than attention/hyperactivity issues.

pages.question: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his parents due to concerns about unusual behaviors that have been occurring for the past 5 years. The parents report that he frequently jerks his head to the side, shrugs his shoulders repeatedly, and makes involuntary humming noises, especially when he is excited or stressed. These behaviors started around age 9, tend to come and go in severity, and do not interfere significantly with his daily activities or school performance.
